profile.summary: Leviticus shows how Israel could live in relation to a holy God through worship, priesthood, sacrifices, and purity norms. For the Christian reader, the book gains light as he points to the work of Christ, who decisively fulfills the priesthood and the atoning sacrifice. Its center is not only ritual, but the revelation of God's holy character and the permanent requirement that his people be holy, living in correct adoration and in concrete love of others.
profile.setting: The setting is the base of Mount Sinai, just after the liberation of Egypt and before the desert walk and the entrance into Canaan. Israel had already received the covenant, the Ten Commandments, the instructions of the tabernacle, and the institution of the priesthood; the tabernacle was already completed and dedicated. At this point in history, God speaks to Moses about his own holiness and about the proper form of worship and conduct for his covenant people.

structure.label: Sacrifices and mediation in the cult
structure.description: Instructions on offerings, atonement and offerings linked to communion with God, highlighting the role of priests and the correct way to approach the Lord.

structure.label: Priestly Consecration
structure.description: Separation and installation of the priesthood, with special emphasis on the ministry of priests before God and the people.

structure.label: Ceremonial Purity and Ordered Life
structure.description: Standards on purity, contamination and restoration, showing how holiness reaches the daily life of the community.

structure.label: Day of the Atonement
structure.description: The great annual rite of atonement, concentrating the need for purification for the people and the sanctuary.

structure.label: Holiness in conviviality and worship
structure.description: Ethical and liturgical guidelines covering human relations, worship practices, holy days, and demands for priests.

structure.label: Holy Times, Commitment and Consecration
structure.description: Calendar of parties, care for worship and final dispositions on votes, values and dedication to the Lord.

themes: The holiness of God and the holiness demanded of his people
Priestly mediation and atonement for sins
Acceptable and reverent worship before God
Love of others as an expression of the covenant with God
readingKeys: Notice how the instructions are not merely ritual: they teach who God is and how his people should approach him.
Note the link between forgiveness before God and ethical responsibility with other people, including poor and foreign.
Read each standard in the light of the central theme: God is holy, and the redemption received by Israel bases the call to live in holiness.
profile.cautions: There is debate about authorship and the date of composition. Some propose a late essay, in the period of exile, while traditional reading and ancient Jewish and Christian testimony attribute the book to Moses, probably during the time in the desert. The introduction also makes it clear that many laws relate to the ancient Israel's culture system; for the Christian reader, its fulfillment in Christ must be affirmed carefully, without erasing the original meaning of the book for Israel.

dossier.narratedEra: Sinai, just after the Exodus, before the pilgrimage in the desert and from the entrance to Canaan. The setting is the foot of Mount Sinai, with the tabernacle already completed and dedicated, and YHWH speaking to Moses to guide a people already freed and in covenant with God (ex 40:34-38; Lv 1:1-2).
dossier.compositionEra: The introduction supports the Mosaic authorship during the desert period, with Leviticus beginning and ending under the mediation of Moses (Lv 1:1-2; 27:34). At the same time, it records the academic proposal of composition in Babylonian exile, about 586-539 BC, but treats it as less convincing; this alternative is presented as a debate, not as consensus.

politics.title: Sovereignty of YHWH instead of human monarchy
politics.detail: The book is set in a community already constituted as a people of the covenant, without human ruler appointed in the introductory passage; the normative authority comes from God, who speaks to Moses and regulates the collective life of Israel. The political context is theocratic: Israel is "special treasure," "priestly kingdom" and separate people for God.
politics.readingImpact: Leviticus' reading does not begin around a king, but around divine sovereignty over worship, purity, and social life. This shifts the attention of state power to the alliance and to priestly mediation.

politics.title: Levitic priestly structure
politics.detail: The notes highlight that the regulations deal mainly with the tribe of Levi, especially the priests descended from Aaron. They officiate, teach the revelation given at Sinai, represent the people before God and are sustained by portions of the offerings.
politics.readingImpact: The context shows that Israel's religion had a defined institutional organization; this prevents reading rites as loose practices and helps to see them as part of a public order of worship and teaching.

politics.title: Contrast with neighboring nations
politics.detail: The introduction explains that peoples of the ancient Near East offered sacrifices to appease their deities and obtain favor; but in Israel the cult did not serve to manipulate God, but to prepare and purify the people in order to approach him.
politics.readingImpact: This contrast changes the reading of the whole sacrificial system: it is neither religious magic nor political bargaining with divinity, but a response to the holiness of God within the covenant.

politics.title: Conquest of Canaan and total exclusion language
politics.detail: Levitico 27 speaks of the Hebrew term kherem in the context of Canaan's conquest war, when cities, animals, and people devoted to other gods were "separated to destruction."
politics.readingImpact: The presence of this reference shows that the final legislation of the book dialogues with Israel's political-military future in the promised land; holiness also appears in relation to war and the occupation of the land.

politics.title: Debate on composition in an exyl context
politics.detail: The introduction mentions the hypothesis that Leviticus was written during Babylonian exile, when Jewish life was already guided further by the synagogue and the rabbi than by the priesthood and the tabernacle. The argument is presented, but rejected in the note as insufficient.
politics.readingImpact: For historical-critical study, this signals a real discussion about the political environment of writing, but also shows that the traditional confessional reading maintains the book's link with the mosaic period.

customs.title: sacrificial system as living pedagogy
customs.detail: Leviticus 1-7 is described as a system in which sacrifices for atonement include burnt offering, a sin offering and guilt; and sacrifices for worship include a meat offering and a peaceful offering. Each offering taught theology through concrete actions.
customs.readingImpact: The cultual context makes the reader realize that legislation is not only ritual technique, but also spiritual formation through gestures, food, blood and fire.

customs.title: Priestly mediation and portions of offers
customs.detail: The priests offered sacrifices in the tabernacle, instructed the people, and received specific parts of the offerings, such as the skin of the burnt offering and certain portions of other sacrifices.
customs.readingImpact: This helps to read the worship of Israel as a system of priestly mediation and sustenance, not as isolated individual devotion.

customs.title: Tabernacle, washing and access to the sacred
customs.detail: The tabernacle is presented as the earthly representation of the palace of God; the Most Holy Place contains the ark as a symbolic throne. Water washing appears as part of the removal of impurities and prerequisite for service in the tabernacle.
customs.readingImpact: The sacred space appears as the center of community life; the reader understands that ritual purity and access to worship are connected to the real presence of God in the midst of the people.

customs.title: Purity, quarantine and return to the community
customs.detail: Notes on Lv 14 describe purification rites for infected people and for homes with mold or rot. The process involved priestly inspection, insulation, washing, blood, fresh water and, in the case of the poor, birds instead of lamb.
customs.readingImpact: The context shows that purity was not only individual; there was a Community, health and social dimension. Impurity suspended participation in offers and the life of the camp, but the goal was reintegration.

customs.title: Votes, rescue and tithes
customs.detail: In Chapter 27, the legislation deals with votes, redemption of people and dedicated goods, a 20% surcharge, and tithes of the product and the herds. There is also special consideration for the poor and the possibility of redemption of certain goods.
customs.readingImpact: The reader realizes that Israel's economic life was integrated into worship: lands, animals, crops and even the social value of people could enter into the logic of consecration and rescue.

language.title: Qorban and the logic of the offer
language.detail: The Hebrew term qorban is explained as a general designation for offerings and gifts, including various types of sacrifice. The note highlights the structure "when/if" in Lv 1:2-6:7, which organizes the legislative material.
language.readingImpact: The word enlarges the semantic field beyond "sacrifice"; the reader sees that the text orders different ways of approaching God, not a single rite.

language.title: Olah as "worst up"
language.detail: The holocaust is explained by the Hebrew "Heavene," alluding to the animal's ascent in smoke and fire. The note also connects the rite to the idea of atonement, ceremonial purification and restoration of communion.
language.readingImpact: The verbal image helps to perceive the emphasis on the movement of the offering to God and the total consummation of the animal, reinforcing the idea of complete delivery.

language.title: "The pleasant aroma" and the language accommodated
language.detail: The expression "pleasant aroma" is explained as culturally situated language: pagan peoples thought that their gods "filled" the offering because they needed it to live; the biblical text uses language, but denies that God needs food.
language.readingImpact: This prevents a materialistic reading of the cult. The phrase does not describe divine necessity, but the acceptance of the offer in relation to holiness and atonement.

language.title: kherem and irrevocable consecration
language.detail: In Lv 27, kherem is described as an irrevocable dedication, and in the context of war as something "separated to destruction." The note emphasizes that what was so devoted was out of common use.
language.readingImpact: Vocabulary shows that "consecrating" can mean different levels of belonging to God: from redeemable offering to irreversible delivery.

language.title: "Declare saint" and the value of words
language.detail: The note on Lv 27 states that the verb translated as "dedica" is strong and means "declares holy." The whole chapter insists that vows made to God should not be treated lightly.
language.readingImpact: The language of the text gives legal and religious weight to human speech; promises are not mere intentions, but acts that create obligations before God.

language.title: Structure of the book framing
language.detail: The book begins and ends with formulas that ascribe the content to God through Moses (Lv 1:1-2; 27:34). The introduction also observes the recurrent pattern "when/if" in sacrificial sections.
language.readingImpact: This literary frame helps the reader see Levitic as continuous and cohesive instruction, not as a loose collection of rules.

timeline.title: Promises to Abraham and exodus as a backdrop
timeline.detail: Leviticus is presented as a continuation of the redemptive history initiated in the promises to Abraham and in the deliverance of Egypt.
timeline.readingImpact: The book should be read as part of a larger history of redemption, not as an isolated handbook of worship.

timeline.title: Sinai, alliance and tabernacle completed
timeline.detail: The immediate scenario is Sinai, after the surrender of the Ten Commandments, the plan of the tabernacle and the institution of the priesthood. The tabernacle had been finished and dedicated when God spoke to Moses.
timeline.readingImpact: The order of reading is clear: first liberation and covenant, then the instruction on how to live before a holy God among the people.

timeline.title: Date of composition debated: desert or exile
timeline.detail: The ancient tradition and the evangelical introduction favor the mosaic writing in the desert after the Exodus. The alternative hypothesis situates the composition in Babylonian exile, approximately between 586 and 539 BC, but this proposal is presented as controversial.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader needs to distinguish narrative setting of the date of writing: the book is set in Sinai, even if the authorship is discussed in the academy.

timeline.title: Completion of the book as a closing milestone
timeline.detail: Leviticus ends with the chapter on vows and tithes and reaffirms the divine origin of the content delivered through Moses.
timeline.readingImpact: The form of closure indicates that the cultual and social legislation is presented as a complete body, enclosed under the authority of God.

investigation: The exact significance of some ritual elements remains unknown, such as the items of the purification rite in Lv 14:4 and certain details of the ceremonies.
The exact distribution of social and economic value in Lv 27 reflects old hierarchies; the note informs the system, but does not solve it historically in all details.
The question of authorship continues to be debated: the Mosaic tradition is affirmed in the notes, but the exile hypothesis appears as an alternative academic proposal.
The exact number and final function of the tithes in Leviticus and Deuteronomy are mentioned as interpreted in different ways by scholars.
The coverage provided is introductory and selective; it highlights sacrificial, purity and vows, but does not comment in depth all Leviticus' legislation.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the annexed notes and therefore depends on a selective coverage of Leviticus: there are more details about sacrifices, purity and vows than about other sections of the book. The historical statements reproduced here come from the secondary sources provided; when they speak of mosaic authorship, Babylonian exile or obscure ritual functions, these are traditions, proposals or inferences within the notes, not independent historical proof. Also, gaps with external knowledge have not been filled, so that some rites, dates and social relations remain described only in the scope in which the sources discuss them.
